lessonTitle: Capturing at scale: taps, mirror ports, drops and retention
md: Monitoring captures other people's data. NIST SP 800-86 advises written policies on what may be monitored without approval, a formal request and approval process before recording a particular user's traffic, warning banners on systems, and rules for handling passwords or private messages that analysts see by accident. Capture only networks you own or are authorised to monitor.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Finding beacons with robust statistics: the RITA approach
md: Medians and quartiles let a beacon survive sleeps, reboots and network outages that wreck a mean. Score regularity robustly, then rank by rarity: a regular connection that only one machine in the company makes is the classic lead.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: IP addresses, subnets and CIDR
md: Prefix length decides everything: which addresses are "local" (same subnet, reached directly) and which need a router. If you can turn /27 into a network address, a broadcast address and a host count, you can read any firewall rule or scan scope.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
md: Remote memory is not slow like disk. It is the same DRAM, reached through one more hop, typically tens of percent slower per miss. The bigger danger is usually *bandwidth*: when all hot data sits on one node, one memory controller serves every socket while the others idle.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
md: Balancing is not free. The kernel docs say the unmapping and extra faults cost overhead that is *ideally* offset by better locality, with no universal guarantee, and that it should be disabled when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes. Workloads that are already pinned and carefully placed are the natural candidates to turn it off.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: Duplicates are handled either after the fact by NMS, a hand-tuned greedy filter on IoU, or during training by one-to-one Hungarian matching, which teaches the model itself to emit one box per object.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
md: Leases and timeouts alone do not fence. A paused process cannot notice that its lease expired while it was paused, so its next write happens anyway. Safety comes from the **storage rejecting** the stale writer: a conditional PUT on a slot the new writer already claimed.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Cardinality: labels multiply, and a histogram multiplies again
md: Never put an unbounded set in a label. The naming guide names the usual offenders: do not use labels to store dimensions with high cardinality, such as user IDs, email addresses, or other unbounded sets of values. Raw URLs with query strings, trace ids, error message strings and timestamps belong on the same list.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: Merging repeats happens **before** removing blanks. Doing it in the other order would turn b - o - o k into b o o k and then merge the o's into 'bok'.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: SELinux: labels, types and the policy that decides
md: Two habits defeat SELinux: switching it to permissive "to make the app work", and feeding every denial to `audit2allow`, a tool that writes allow rules from log lines. The SELinux Notebook warns that new rules "may start opening holes". First ask whether the label is wrong (restorecon) or a boolean exists for the need.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: What OSINT is, and what it is for
md: OSINT is not "anything on the internet is fair game". Collecting and combining public facts about a private person to expose, harass or locate them is **doxxing** (publishing documents and personal details about someone) and can be a crime and is always a harm. This course does not teach it.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Mapping your own organisation's public footprint
md: Point OSINT at yourself first. Registration data, DNS, certificate logs, search engines, code hosts and job adverts together describe what an attacker sees; an inventory diffed on a schedule turns that into findings.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Archiving: capturing evidence that will still be trusted later
md: Capture URL, source, full-page image and media; record who, when (UTC, synced clock) and why; hash every file at collection; keep a read-only copy.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build
md: `cmake -S . -B build` configures and generates; `cmake --build build` runs the native tool. Settings live in `build/CMakeCache.txt` and persist until you change them, remove them, or use `--fresh`.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
md: Retrying until green is not fixing. The same math that removes noise also removes signal from real intermittent bugs, and concurrency bugs are exactly the ones that fail intermittently. Google's post makes a related point about its own fail three times in a row policy: it reduces false positives but encourages developers to ignore flakiness and delays finding real breakages.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: GitHub mechanics: decisions, suggestions and merge rules
md: Do not resolve a reviewer's thread you disagreed with and did not change. Collapsing a thread hides it from the list of open conversations, so silently resolving an open disagreement reads as ignoring it. Reply, and resolve only when the thread is truly finished.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
md: Default to public communication, with two exceptions: security vulnerabilities and serious conduct violations. Each has its own documented private channel; find it before you need it.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
md: `git commit --fixup=X` then `git rebase -i --autosquash BASE` puts a fix into commit X without editing the todo list by hand. Every commit after X gets a new hash.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
md: Copyleft obligations trigger on conveying: giving someone a copy. AGPL is the exception that also counts remote network use of a modified version.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
md: A small, very stable difference can still be a layout accident: your patch moved code, and alignment changed. If a 1 to 2% win appears in code you did not expect to matter, rebuild with a different layout (the paper calls this setup randomization) or test on another machine before claiming it.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: git blame: who last changed a line, and seeing past noise
md: blame only describes lines that exist now. The manual is explicit: the report does "not tell you anything about lines which have been deleted or replaced". If you want to know when a check was removed, blame cannot answer; the next lesson's pickaxe can.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
md: A fast, exact repro turns history into a binary search: about $\log_2 N$ automated tests to find the commit that introduced the bug, and naming that commit in your report saves the maintainer hours.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: A title and description that explain why
md: Title: what the change does, short enough for one-line views. Body: the problem and its impact, the approach, where to look, what you left out, and links. The description outlives the review: Google notes it may be read by hundreds of people over the years.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: A cache hit needs the whole prefix up to a block boundary to match. Chained hashes make that a sequence of dictionary lookups, and keeping freed blocks cached until they are actually reallocated makes eviction LRU for free.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Active scanning: host discovery and what each probe tells you
md: Open means a program answered. Closed means the host answered but nothing listens. Filtered means something in between dropped or refused the probe. Open|filtered means silence that could be either. Every state is information about both the host and the firewall in front of it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: A wide box does not mean each call is slow. It may be cheap but called very often. The flame graph cannot tell the difference because sampling never sees call counts.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Transactions: how libpmemobj's undo log survives a crash
md: A libpmemobj transaction is about crash atomicity, not isolation. The manual is explicit: "transactions do not provide atomicity with respect to other threads". Changes are visible to other threads immediately, so you still need locks (libpmemobj offers persistent-memory-resident mutexes for this).

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Reading headers to triage a suspicious message
md: RFC 8601 says a border server MUST delete any Authentication-Results header that claims its own authserv-id but did not come from a trusted server, and that mail apps should ignore these headers unless the hostname is on an explicit trusted list. Trust exactly one: the topmost from your own authserv-id.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Strict aliasing: which pointer casts C lets you read through
md: "It works in my debug build" proves nothing here. Aliasing bugs are invisible at -O0 and appear only when the optimizer uses the rule, often after an unrelated change lets it inline a function. Like the misaligned cast in lesson 4, the bug is in the source, whatever the build happens to do.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Backbones, top-down versus bottom-up, and part affinity fields
md: Bottom-up is not free of crowd effects. The CNN pass is constant, but the number of candidate pairs per limb grows with the number of people, and the whole image goes through the network at one input size, so small, distant people cover only a few heatmap pixels, while top-down resizes every person to the same crop size.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Inside ML-KEM: modules, compression and the FO transform
md: Name the keys the way FIPS 203 does: **encapsulation key** (ek, public) and **decapsulation key** (dk, secret). ML-KEM.KeyGen starts from two random 32-byte seeds $(d, z)$, and Go's crypto/mlkem stores just this 64-byte seed as the private key; OpenSSL's default private-key file holds the seed plus the expanded decapsulation key. The seed regenerates everything, so protect it exactly like the full decapsulation key.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Filtering during traversal is the right default for medium selectivity, but it has two failure modes at low $s$: a strict walk gets cut off (disconnection), and a walk-through degenerates into visiting about $k/s$ nodes. Both point to the same escape hatch: when matches are few, scan them directly.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
md: Privacy engineering reviews every data action, not only every attacker. NIST's objectives give the questions: will people be surprised (predictability), can we find and change or delete one person's data (manageability), and does the system know who is who more than it needs to (disassociability)?

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: When k-anonymity fails: l-diversity and t-closeness
md: l-diversity and t-closeness reduce attribute disclosure in one table under one attacker model. They do not compose across releases and they give no guarantee against unanticipated background knowledge.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Case: the 2020 US Census adopts differential privacy
md: A published epsilon is a starting point for review, not a verdict. Ask what the unit of privacy is, how the budget is split across tables and geographies, and what error users can tolerate. The Census case shows that both privacy and accuracy are political as well as technical choices.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Data protection impact assessments that change the design
md: A DPIA written after launch, or one whose risk section lists only security threats to the company, misses the point. It must be done before processing, assess necessity, and score harm to the individuals in the data.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 1: unquoted paths and weak service permissions
md: Run the path audit and the ACL audit together. An unquoted path with no writable folder before it is a hygiene fix; with one, it is a working escalation to SYSTEM.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Build it: train a small PRM and rerank with it
md: A PRM is a token classifier whose labels sit only on step separators; the rest of the sequence is ignored by the loss. Train and score with identical tokenization, then judge it two ways: does it pick better answers, and does it find the first wrong step.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
md: Misconception: "threads are cheap because the kernel treats them as lighter objects." On Linux a thread and a process are the same kind of task. A thread is cheaper to create because there is less to set up (no new address space or page tables), and switching between two threads of one process is cheaper because the address space stays loaded. Those savings come from sharing, not from a different kind of object.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
md: PQ builds an exponentially large codebook, $(k^*)^m$ centroids, out of $m$ tiny ones. Each vector costs $m \log_2 k^*$ bits no matter how many dimensions it has.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
md: A rewrite produced without evaluation data is a hypothesis, not a result. Treat it like a candidate from a proposer: score it on your validation set against the current prompt before shipping.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
md: Text is characters, bytes are numbers. Decode at the edge of your program (when you read), work with `str` inside, and encode again only when you hash, send or write bytes.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Encoding is reversible formatting, not secrecy. Normalize data (decode, lowercase, refang) before matching it, and expect attackers to stack encodings to slip past exact-match rules.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE
md: These numbers come from specific benchmarks (MS MARCO, TREC DL) and specific models. Measure on your own queries with judged results before adopting any expansion: a gain on average can still hurt many individual queries.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: RaBitQ indexing: center and normalize, apply one random rotation, store the sign bits plus two floats per vector. The codebook is the rotated hypercube, so no k-means training is needed.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Workflows as state machines: skipping, repeating and reordering steps
md: Enforce workflows as explicit state machines on the server. For every request ask: is this action allowed from the state this object is in right now? If the only thing enforcing the order is the user interface, the order is not enforced.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Idempotency keys: safe retries, and what they do not stop
md: Look at line four of the output. Idempotency keys are chosen by the client, so an attacker racing a coupon or a withdrawal simply sends a different key with each request. Keys make honest retries safe; they do nothing for limits. The limit itself still needs lesson 9's atomic check.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Paxos: choosing one value with prepare and accept
md: A Paxos proposer is not free to pick its value. After phase 1 it must adopt the value of the highest-numbered proposal any acceptor in its majority reports. That single rule is what keeps a chosen value from ever changing.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
md: A citation is a claim, not a proof. The model can attach [3] to a sentence [3] does not support, as it did here. ALCE found even the best models lacked complete citation support about 50% of the time on ELI5 (Explain Like I'm Five: open-ended how and why questions from a Reddit forum), so check citations automatically rather than trusting their presence.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: Every cutoff metric hides a choice: the cutoff, the relevance threshold (grade at least 1 here), the divisor, and what to do with short runs. Two papers both reporting "MAP@10" may be computing different numbers.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The way in: brokers, stolen logins and edge devices
md: MFA is necessary and not sufficient. Session theft (Citrix Bleed), help desk resets and unpatched appliances all walk past a password-plus-code login. Close each door with the control that fits it, and verify by testing, not by policy.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
md: RDMA is not "the OS is gone". The kernel driver still creates queues, pins and maps memory, and handles errors. What disappears is per-message kernel work. That split between a slow **control path** and a fast **data path** is the design of the whole API.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
md: An authoritative server makes the server state the only truth. Every latency trick in the next lessons changes only what the *client displays*; none of them lets a client decide the outcome.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
md: Do not drop the zeros. Training only on observed implicit events (all with p = 1) lets the model predict 1 everywhere and still reach zero loss. The low-confidence zeros are what make the scores discriminative.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
md: A common misconception is that the pixels-per-mm method only fails at extreme angles. In this toy, a moderate 40 degree tilt already puts it 15 percent off. Under perspective, scale varies with both position and direction across the plane.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The planner is only as good as its row estimates. It searches join orders exhaustively by dynamic programming up to a limit, then genetically; but a 100x row misestimate can turn the cheapest-looking plan into the slowest. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE estimates against actuals first.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
md: Unhackability is a very strong condition. For rich policy classes, every proxy that is not simply equivalent to the true reward (same ranking of all policies) can be hacked by some policy. Skalse et al. conclude that learned rewards are better treated as aids to policy learning than as specifications to optimize without limit. The practical question becomes how far you can optimize before hacking appears.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: From gaming to tampering: reward tampering and in-context hacking
md: Misconception: reward hacking only happens during RL training. ICRH needs no gradient at all. An agent with frozen weights, a goal and a feedback loop optimizes in context, and its side effects grow with each cycle.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
md: Simulate, do not multiply point estimates. The mean of the simulation is the ALE; the percentiles describe bad years; and a typical year (the median) may cost nothing at all, which is exactly why risk without numbers is easy to ignore until it happens.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
md: Read the **exceptions** and the **complementary user entity controls** (CUECs) sections of any vendor's SOC 2. Exceptions are where the auditor found a control did not operate. CUECs are controls the vendor assumes *you* perform (for example, "customers are responsible for enabling MFA for their users"); if you do not, the vendor's report does not cover that risk.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Third-party risk: questionnaires, SBOMs and concentration risk
md: A questionnaire is a vendor's own claims. "Yes" to every question from a 20-person startup is a signal to ask for evidence, not a pass. And a vendor that is excellent at security can still be a concentration risk: CrowdStrike was the security control, not the attacker. Score both "how likely is this vendor to be breached" and "what happens to us if this vendor stops working for a day".

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: A common misconception is that a bigger training cluster speeds up RL roughly linearly. Training is often a minority of the step. If generation is two-thirds of the time, even infinitely fast training saves at most a third.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Measuring achieved bandwidth with a copy kernel
md:
Common traps:
- **Arrays that fit in L2.** An 8 MB array on an H100 (50 MB L2) measures cache bandwidth, not HBM.
- **Mixing GB and GiB.** 2,982.6 GB/s is 2,777.8 GiB/s. Use one divisor for both theory and measurement.
- **Timing the first launch** or using host timers without synchronizing.
- **Uncoalesced or strided access**, which measures your access pattern, not the memory.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: RRF needs only positions. Scores on different scales, scores that drift between index versions, even systems that expose no scores at all can be fused, because $1/(k + r)$ is the same function of rank for every input.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Unsafe code is concentrated in reviewed subsystem abstractions. A driver written only against those abstractions cannot cause undefined behavior, *provided the abstractions are sound* and every `unsafe` block honours its contract. That proviso is the whole game; lesson 10 shows what happens when it fails.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: What Rust in the kernel does not prevent, and what it costs
md: Misconception: "written in Rust" means "free of memory corruption". A soundness bug in one `unsafe` block can corrupt memory exactly like C. What changes is *where to look*: the bug was in an unsafe block with a written, checkable claim, not anywhere in thousands of lines of driver logic.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: Weighted vtime in sched_ext takes a few lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Whether the weights actually hold depends on whether prev competes in `dispatch`; `scx_simple`'s does not, so on one CPU no task gets more than half.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production
md: Ignoring kernel bugs, the kernel's tools/sched_ext README puts the worst case plainly: a broken sched_ext scheduler can starve some threads until the watchdog fires. It cannot corrupt memory, and the machine returns to the fair scheduler on its own.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key hierarchies in KMS: envelope encryption and rotating the KEK
md: Two different jobs share the word rotation. Rotating a KEK limits the amount of data under one key version and lets old versions eventually be retired. Revoking access (permissions, sessions, leases) is what stops a thief. Plan both.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
md: Pickle shows up in places reviewers forget: cache layers, task queues, session stores, and machine learning model files, which are often pickles inside. "It only comes from our own cache" is true only until someone else can write to that cache.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Go: nil maps, data races and the race detector
md: Go is memory-safe only for race-free programs. In every diff, find state shared between goroutines (globals, maps in structs, caches) and confirm one lock or channel owns it. Run tests with -race, and remember it only sees the paths your tests execute.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: White-box review of a small app, end to end
md: A baseline review is the four questions applied systematically: list every entry point, check authentication and authorization on each, trace every input to every sink, then sweep the language's hazards. Tools find the dangerous calls; only the reviewer finds the missing checks.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: When the state machine forgets: Erlang/OTP SSH (CVE-2025-32433)
md: Default deny applies to protocol states as much as to firewall rules: for each state, list the messages that are allowed and reject everything else. A dispatcher that looks only at the message type is an authentication bypass waiting for someone to send messages out of order.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions and separation of duty
md: Giving a reporting job or an engineer direct write access to production tables quietly turns them into an uncertified TP. Read-only replicas for reporting, and audited break-glass access for emergencies, keep rule E1 true.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
md: Mitigation is not remediation. Volexity's disclosure warned that a mitigation "does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise". After an edge device is exploited, assume its secrets and its users' credentials are gone, and rotate them.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Testing and running automations: dry runs, caps and staged rollout
md: Put validation, never-act lists, caps, idempotency and dry run inside the action function; test the failure paths and hostile inputs; roll out in stages; and alert when an automation goes quiet.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
md: Before asking "is this secure?", ask "which asset, and which property: confidentiality, integrity or availability?" Different properties need different defences: encryption (scrambling data so only holders of a secret key can read it) mostly protects confidentiality, hashes and signatures protect integrity and authenticity, and backups and redundancy protect availability.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
md: The leak did not create the vulnerability; it created a free, reliable exploit. By the time WannaCry hit, the patch had existed for 59 days. Treat every critical advisory as if working exploit code will be public soon, because sometimes it already is.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
md: Authorisation is the line. Own it or get written, scoped permission; stop at other people's data; report privately and give owners time to fix. Practise on platforms built for it.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions
md: Do not present fear or vanity. Breach headlines from other companies and "millions of attacks blocked" both waste the board's attention. Directors respond to clear risk, honest measures and a specific ask, and they remember who was straight with them.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
md: A self-improvement loop is only as good as its filter. The precision of the check sets the quality of the kept data, and the set of problems the model can sometimes solve sets how far the loop can reach.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
md: Never let the cache cross users for answers that depend on who is asking: balances, orders, permissions, anything personal. A false hit there is not a quality bug; it is a data leak. Scope by user or tenant, or bypass the cache for those requests entirely.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
md: Turning off DTDs (DOCTYPE declarations) removes the whole feature: no DTD, no entity declarations, so no external entity fetch and no billion laughs. OWASP's first rule is to disable DTDs whenever possible, and to keep XInclude off too, since it loads documents without any DTD. If a format truly needs DTDs, disable external entities and external DTD loading explicitly, and keep the parser library up to date.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Scheduling cannot create reuse; it can only avoid destroying it. The DFS bound (sum of tree edges) is the floor on prefill work, and ordering decides whether a tight cache reaches it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: A SIMD register is a small array of lanes. One instruction does the same operation on every lane. Lane count = register width / element width, so 4, 8 or 16 floats for 128, 256 or 512 bits. Vertical (lane-wise) work is cheap; horizontal (across-lane) work costs shuffles.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
md: Compile for what you can require, dispatch for what you cannot. -march levels give the compiler AVX2 or AVX-512 everywhere but crash on older CPUs; target_clones, __builtin_cpu_supports or is_x86_feature_detected! pick the best version per machine at run time.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: Colocation saves GPUs and keeps every GPU busy in a synchronous loop, but it forces phases to take turns and requires offloading. Separate pools only win if you also overlap rollout with training; on their own they just double the GPU count.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The four triage questions, and the decision flow they make
md: "Expected" needs evidence: a ticket, a calendar entry, a confirmation through a channel the attacker does not control. "The user is an admin, admins do this" is a guess. Attackers who steal admin accounts do exactly what admins do.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
md: Do not "watch it to learn more" once you see encryption or recovery tampering. Every minute of observation costs files. Escalate immediately with what you know, isolate if your playbook allows it, and let incident response decide about wider containment.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
md: Do not ask people to detect lies in real time. Give them a rule that does not depend on the caller being honest, and make following the rule faster than arguing.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
md: The people layer is defended by design (processes that do not depend on spotting lies), by technology that makes mistakes harmless, and by a culture where reporting is fast, safe and thanked. Blame breaks all three.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: Judge an SAE by sparsity (L0), reconstruction (FVU) and downstream loss together, then verify interpretations causally. Steering by clamping a latent equals adding $(c - f_i)$ times its decoder direction while keeping the SAE error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
md: Negative weights mean an ordinary kriging estimate can fall outside the range of the readings. That can be right for a smooth field with a peak between sensors, but for quantities that must stay positive (rainfall, concentrations) check for negative predictions.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
md: Speedup is not tokens per pass. A draft that is accurate but slow (high alpha, high c) can lose to a weaker but nearly free one. Leviathan et al. found drafts about two orders of magnitude smaller than the target usually balanced alpha and c best.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Silence is where a language-model decoder is least constrained by audio. Short clips are padded to 30 s, long pauses leave long stretches of nothing, and the decoder can fill them with plausible web-caption text. The repetition and confidence checks do not catch a fluent, confident invented sentence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation
md: Thread caches are a memory-for-speed trade. jemalloc's manual says it plainly: caching makes allocation very fast but increases memory use and fragmentation, since some objects stay parked in each thread's cache. TCMalloc moved to per-CPU caches because per-thread caches made footprint grow with the number of threads.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
md: Little free memory is not a problem by itself. The page cache deliberately fills idle RAM with file data, and clean cached pages are reclaimable at any moment. Trouble shows up as rates: sustained swap-in and swap-out in `vmstat`, major faults per second, and processes stalled in direct reclaim.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Kafka turns backpressure from data loss into delay: as long as retention covers the backlog, a slow consumer only falls behind. The bounded buffers inside the processor are what make the slowdown propagate instead of growing memory without bound.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Scaling by the square root of d_k is not mainly about float overflow (implementations subtract the row max before exponentiating anyway). It keeps softmax out of its saturated, near one-hot region so gradients stay usable as d_k grows.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
md: Teacher forcing is a training trick. At inference the decoder only ever sees its own earlier outputs, mistakes included, and the encoder output is computed once per source sentence, not once per step.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25's IDF and a full worked example
md: BM25 = sum over query terms of IDF x f / (f + k1 x (1 - b + b x |d| / avgdl)). Three statistics per term and document: f, |d|, and n_t; two per collection: N and avgdl.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: Never compare losses across tokenizers. 1.47 nats per *character* and 2.85 nats per *BPE token* measure different things: a BPE token covers several characters, so it is much harder to predict. The released GPT-2 scores 3.12 on OWT partly because it was trained on WebText, not OpenWebText; nanoGPT notes that fine-tuning it on OWT brings it to about 2.85.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
md: A density value is not a probability, so it can be larger than 1. A density squeezed onto a narrow range must be tall to keep its total area at 1: spread evenly over an interval of width 0.5, its height is 2. Only areas under a density are probabilities.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Second derivatives, the Hessian and the shape of a minimum
md: The Hessian holds the curvature in every direction. Its eigenvalues classify a critical point (all positive: minimum; mixed signs: saddle), the largest one sets the stable learning rate $2/\lambda_{\max}$, and their ratio sets how slowly gradient descent converges.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
md: Inside `[ ]`, quote every variable: `[ "$x" = foo ]`. An empty or spaced value otherwise changes how many arguments `[` receives, and the test fails with an error instead of returning false. Inside `[[ ]]` a variable needs no quotes, except on the right of `==` or `=~`: there quotes make the pattern literal, so `[[ $f == "*.log" ]]` matches only a file named `*.log`.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: Status 0 means success; 128 + N means killed by signal N. Start scripts with `set -euo pipefail`, quote every expansion, send errors to fd 2, and exit non-zero on failure so the next tool in the chain can tell.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Vector arithmetic analogies are a nice demo, not a law. The answer depends on excluding inputs, and Nissim et al. show that other implementation choices (casing, frequency cutoffs, the exact formula) change results too. The same arithmetic surfaces social biases: Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found that the GoogleNews word2vec vectors complete *man : computer programmer :: woman : x* with *homemaker*.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline
md: Intensity counts HBM traffic, not every load. Good kernels tile data into shared memory and registers so each HBM byte is reused many times; a naive kernel that re-reads HBM has a much lower effective intensity than the formula suggests.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: Misconception: "the compiler makes something the CPU runs straight off the disk." The CPU only fetches instructions from memory. An executable is inert until the OS loader maps it into a process's memory and points the CPU at its entry point.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
md: A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
md: Preference data is a design choice: who labels, under which guidelines, on which prompts, with which ratings. Separate signals (helpfulness and safety) and AI labels from written principles (RLAIF) are now standard ingredients of post-training.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: tf rewards a term repeated inside the document; idf rewards a term that is rare across the collection. TF-IDF multiplies them, so a match counts most when the term is frequent here and rare elsewhere.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
md: Compile each `.c` file separately into a `.o`, then link them. The preprocessor pastes text, the compiler checks one translation unit at a time, and the linker joins units together by symbol name.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
md: Narrow types promote to int before arithmetic; mixed signed and unsigned operands usually become unsigned; conversion to unsigned wraps modulo 2 to the width. Compile with `-Wall -Wextra` and read every sign warning.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
md: Check every return value from a library call. On failure, errno says why; perror and strerror turn it into text. Release resources on every path, typically through one cleanup label, and report the outcome through the exit status.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: A move is not a deep copy and not a pointer trick at run time. It is a shallow copy of the value's bytes **plus** a compile-time rule that the source is dead. The heap block never moves.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
md: A lifetime parameter on a struct marks it as a view into data it does not own, and the checker keeps every use of the view inside the data's lifetime. Return `&'a T` from a method to tie the result to the data rather than to the struct.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = \sum_i a_i b_i = \|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\theta$. Its sign says whether two vectors point the same way (positive), at right angles (zero), or opposite (negative). Cosine similarity is the dot product with lengths divided out.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: directions a matrix only stretches
md: $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$: eigenvectors are the directions $A$ only stretches, eigenvalues the stretch factors, found from $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. Repeated multiplication is dominated by the largest $|\lambda|$. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors: $S = Q\Lambda Q^\top$.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: stepping downhill, and how big a step
md: Gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla L$. On a quadratic, each step multiplies the error by $1 - \eta\lambda$ per direction, so it converges only if $\eta < 2/\lambda$ for every curvature $\lambda$, and the sharpest direction sets the limit.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Bias and variance: where the U-shaped test curve comes from
md: Expected test error = bias squared + variance + noise. Simple models miss systematically (bias), flexible models chase noise (variance), and the noise sets a floor nobody can beat. Regularization and more data mainly cut variance.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Build it: a complete training loop in NumPy
md: A complete training loop is: split, fit preprocessing on train, shuffle each epoch, step on minibatch gradients plus the penalty gradient, watch validation loss, keep the best weights, and evaluate on test once. Every bug in later, bigger models is a violation of one of these steps.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backprop for a mini-batch, in matrix form
md: A batched gradient is the per-example gradient summed (or averaged) over the rows of the batch. The transposes are just how a matrix product writes that sum, and a quick check that every gradient has the shape of its parameter catches most mistakes.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time
md: No policy wins on every metric. SJF and STCF minimize average turnaround but give long waits before a job first runs; round robin gives fast response but stretches every job's completion. Choosing a scheduler means choosing which metric you care about.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
md: Most concurrency bugs are atomicity violations (fix: a lock around the whole check-then-act) or order violations (fix: a condition variable on a state variable). Deadlock needs four conditions; the usual cure is to acquire locks in one global order.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Describing data: mean, median, percentiles and outliers
md: The mean answers "total divided by count", the median answers "what is typical", and tail percentiles answer "how bad is it for the unlucky few". For skewed data, report more than the mean.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions
md: The CDF turns any range question into a subtraction, $F(b) - F(a)$. Standardizing turns any normal question into the standard normal CDF, $\Phi$.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
md: The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement lists the usual misreadings. A p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true (that is the Bayes' rule mix-up from lesson 3), it does **not** measure the size or importance of an effect, and decisions should not rest only on whether it crosses 0.05. Report the effect size (here the 2 point gap) and its confidence interval.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal means lowest loss **per training FLOP**. It says nothing about the cost of serving the model afterwards, and the 20x ratio is tied to the data, architecture and training recipe it was measured on.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: In-batch negatives assume the other passages are wrong. If the batch holds two copies of the same passage, or two paraphrased questions, the loss pushes a correct answer away. sentence-transformers recommends the `NO_DUPLICATES` batch sampler, which never puts the same text twice in one batch, for this reason. Hard negatives mined automatically can also be unlabeled positives, so they need filtering.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
md: Encoding is **not** "find the longest matching token from the left" and not "pick the segmentation with fewest tokens". BPE applies merges greedily in the order they were learned. A different procedure over the same vocabulary can give a different split, and the model was trained on BPE's split.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
md: Initialization is about **variance, not values**. Pick the weight scale so that each layer multiplies the activation variance (and the gradient variance) by about 1. For ReLU that means $\mathrm{Var}(w) = 2/\text{fan-in}$; with depth, any other factor compounds exponentially.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
md: Every check has a **known right answer**: loss at init equals $\ln C$, one batch overfits to about zero, the real model beats an input-independent baseline. Add one piece of complexity at a time and re-check, so when something breaks you know which change did it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: The software supply chain: a map with every attack point
md: Every stage is a trust boundary, and attackers pick the stage with the widest fan-out: one poisoned library, build server or CI action reaches thousands of victims at once. Defence means asking, for each arrow, what proves the thing arriving is the thing you expected.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
md: Provenance moves the question from 'do I trust this file?' to 'do I trust this repository, this workflow and this build platform?', which you can check by machine. npm's documentation is explicit that provenance does not guarantee a package has no malicious code; it makes origin verifiable.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: Accumulation is not a free pass. The bound depends on the original real data never being thrown away, and on synthetic data being added on top rather than diluting a fixed budget: a variant that trains on n times more pure synthetic data still diverges, only more slowly (logarithmically). MAD also reports that a fixed real set only delayed degradation in its image experiments.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: A system call is a mode switch plus cache pollution, paid per call. Make fewer, bigger calls (buffering, vectored I/O, batching) and let the vDSO serve the hottest read-only queries without entering the kernel.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd
md: To share writable memory, both processes need `MAP_SHARED` mappings of the same pages: anonymous before `fork`, a `shm_open` name, or a memfd descriptor. Then order the accesses with release and acquire atomics or a lock; the mapping itself guarantees no ordering at all.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
md: Latency = completion time minus *intended* start time. The intended start comes from a load plan that does not depend on how fast the server answers.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time scaling has two halves that can fail independently. **Coverage**: does any attempt contain a correct answer? **Precision**: can you pick it out? The next two lessons take them one at a time.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Tree search for reasoning: Tree of Thoughts, MCTS, inference laws
md: Tree search pays when you have a step-level evaluator you can trust (code that runs, a checked answer, a strong PRM) and when early mistakes are expensive, as in Game of 24. With a weak evaluator, more search mostly finds the evaluator's mistakes, the over-optimization seen in lesson 5. And always compare at equal compute: rollouts are not free.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
md: One step of online gradient descent (one gradient step per token, in arrival order) on the regression loss is exactly the DeltaNet update with $\beta = \eta$. The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
md: Per-CPU does not automatically mean scalable. The paper found that padding and aligning each CPU's structure to its own cache line was critical for linear scaling. Without it, the per-CPU counters of neighbouring CPUs share a line and you are back to cache line ping-pong through false sharing.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
md: LOTL hunts are baseline hunts in disguise. The tools are legitimate, so the evidence is never the tool alone: it is the tool used by an account, on a host, at a time, or in a sequence that this environment has not seen before.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code
md: Do not average the two grades into one number, and do not let the letter drive the digit. "A5" (a reliable source passing on something improbable) is a perfectly valid and useful grade: it tells the reader to check before acting, whoever sent it.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Writing an intelligence product people act on
md: A good intelligence product states a judgement, says how likely and how sure in standard words, shows the evidence and its grade, tells each reader what to do and by when, admits its gaps, and asks for feedback. Everything else in CTI exists to make that page right.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles I: simple, closed by default, checked every time
md: Default deny, check every request in one place, keep that place small, and assume the attacker has read the code. Most broken access control bugs violate at least one of these four.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: CXL can hold *warm* data because a miss there costs about 2x DRAM. Swap can only hold *cold* data because a miss there costs about 100x to 400x. That is why demotion tries CXL first and swap last.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
md: The padlock icon means "this connection is encrypted to the named site", not "this site is safe". Phishing sites get valid certificates for their own domains in seconds.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Mutual TLS and running your own internal CA
md: mTLS answers "which service is calling?". It does not answer "is this service allowed to do this?". Authorization (orders may charge, but not refund) is still your application's job, keyed on the verified identity.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
md: An image is not one token. It is hundreds to thousands of positions in the same context window as the text, and that count grows with the square of the resolution. Every unified design is constrained by this budget.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is not a container. A container shares the host's Linux kernel and is isolated by kernel features (namespaces, which give a process its own view of process ids, mounts and network, and cgroups, control groups that cap its CPU, memory and I/O). A unikernel is a real VM with its own tiny kernel, isolated by hardware virtualization.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
md: Unikernels trade **generality for specialization**: fewer layers, smaller images, faster boots and cheaper calls, paid for with porting work, partial POSIX, no processes, weaker tooling and security that depends entirely on what the libOS implements.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Segments: immutable indexes, a write buffer, tombstones and merges
md: Immutable segments turn random in-place updates into sequential writes plus background rewrites. The price is read amplification: every query touches every segment, and dead rows cost time until a merge removes them.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
md: Remember the condition that makes resharding free: choose generation groups so that **each GPU's generation shard contains its training shard**. Then the only traffic is one all-gather per micro DP group, and no GPU keeps a second copy.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT
md: Generating a frame is not one forward pass. Each frame costs a full MaskGIT loop (25 passes in Genie) over a context that grows with every frame. The paper's own limitations: Genie runs at around 1 FPS and is limited to 16 frames of memory.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Decide by data and shift. Little data or a frozen-feature baseline needed: linear probe. Many tasks on one backbone or tight memory: LoRA (adapters are tiny and merge for free). Plenty of data from the deployment distribution: full fine-tune. Expect distribution shift at deployment: probe first, then fine-tune (LP-FT).

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
md: A common misreading is that the straight-through estimator makes quantization differentiable. It does not: it substitutes the identity gradient. The encoder is updated as if the decoder had received $z_e$, which is a useful but biased approximation that is better when $z_e$ stays close to its code.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
md: A mixed batch is one flat list of tokens plus offsets. Backends with one variable-length kernel use it as is. Backends with separate decode and prefill kernels ask for decodes first, so one index splits the batch.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
md: Resizing is silent by default. If your receipt is downscaled, small digits may become unreadable and any coordinates the model returns refer to the resized image. Anthropic's docs recommend resizing yourself first; OpenAI's guide notes images may be resized even with original detail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: The template for almost every wait-free algorithm since: **announce** your operation in a per-thread slot, then **help** pending operations in an order that guarantees each announced operation gets its turn within a bounded number of steps.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: Every global score is an area-weighted average. Weights proportional to cos(latitude) count each unit of Earth's surface once.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
md: Lockout and reset tests act on accounts. Run them only on accounts you created. A lockout test against a real user's account is a denial of service against that person.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
md: Write for three readers: the triager reproduces, the engineer fixes, the lead prioritises. Exact steps with your own accounts, evidence, plausible impact, reasoned severity, a suggested fix, and no one else's data.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust
md: CSP is defence in depth, not a fix. A permissive policy with `'unsafe-inline'` stops almost nothing, and even a strict policy cannot help if your own trusted script takes attacker text and passes it to `eval()` or builds script elements from it. Encode output and validate input first; then add CSP.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
md: Because the walk stops early, ACE order changes the result. Windows tools keep a canonical order: explicit denies, then explicit allows, then inherited denies, then inherited allows. Hand-built DACLs in the wrong order can grant access you meant to deny.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
md: Changing the passphrase does not protect recordings already made: if an old passphrase is later guessed, every handshake recorded under it can be replayed into the PTK computation. With WPA2-Personal, the passphrase protects the past as well as the future.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
md: Leave certificate validation to the platform. The bug is almost always code that disables it: an empty trust manager, an always-true hostname verifier, a delegate that trusts any server, or a blanket ATS or cleartext exception. Pin only endpoints you control, and always ship a backup pin. Pins outlive app releases: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030, so plan rotation to post-quantum keys.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
md: sendfile shares page cache pages with the network stack. The man page warns that the transferred part of the file must stay unmodified until the reader on the other end has consumed it. If another process rewrites the file mid-send, the bytes on the wire can be a mix of old and new.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Two details. First, the bars show W p renormalized to sum to 1 for readability; the paper writes softmax(W p + b), which gives different numbers (T2 sports 0.911) but the same argmax, and the paper predicts with the argmax. Second, the bias is contextual: change the instruction, the examples, or their order, and p_cf must be measured again.
